name: Magar
confidence_why: The only remark on accent is Beames 1870's impression that Magar has 'no peculiarities of accent' and a 'level and even' pronunciation, Subba 1972 states that no study of accent was made, and Grierson 1909, Hale 1973 and Baskaran 2009 say nothing about stress, so the word-stress system of Magar remains unknown.
catalog_citation: Beames, John. 1870. Art. IV. On the Magar Language of Nepal. Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland, New Series 4: 178-228 (paper read 16 Nov 1868).
catalog_locator: Part II, Section 1 'Sounds', p. 190 (last two paragraphs before 'Section 2. The Noun'); archive.org item journalofroyalas4187roya
catalog_quote: The distinction between long and short vowels is only clearly marked in words of Hindi origin. In pure Magar words there is very little distinction. The language in this respect also follows the usage of Tibetan. There are no peculiarities of accent beyond a slight drawl at the end of a sentence. The pronunciation is level and even, though somewhat indistinct, the words short and simple, and the general effect of the language on the ear is soft and musical.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Beames reports no noticeable word accent at all: pronunciation is 'level and even', the only prominence effect being a slight lengthening ('drawl') at the end of a sentence. No syllable is singled out as stressed, so no placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only qualification is the sentence-final drawl
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic 1870 remark in a 'Sounds' section, covering connected speech as a whole (sentence-final drawl is phrase-level); not a phonological analysis. The two 20th-century analyses that were readable are silent: Subba 1972 (p. 3) states outright that accent and intonation were not studied, and the SIL-based Magar note in Hale 1973 (pp. 18-19) discusses breathiness and pitch lowering but says nothing about stress. The modern reference grammar (Grunow-Hårsta 2008) could not be opened.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: Beames 1870 (the quoted source) worked with two Magar soldiers supplied by Jung Bahadur through the Kathmandu Residency and does not name their home district; Glottolog files the sketch under east2352 (Eastern Magar, mgp). The other readable descriptions are also eastern: Subba 1972's principal informant is from Rising, Tanahu; the SIL note in Hale 1973 (after Shepherd & Shepherd 1971) describes Yanchok, Tanahu; Baskaran 2009 describes Sikkim 'Mangari'. Western Magar (Palpa/Syangja/Rolpa etc.) is west2418 [mrd], checked separately in

tone_statements.citation: Hilty, Holly J. 2013. Sociolinguistic Survey of Eastern Magar in Nepal. Kathmandu: Linguistic Survey of Nepal (LinSuN), Central Department of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University & SIL International. 67 pp. (+ Appendices, 124 pp.). SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 53996.
tone_statements.quote: Shepherd states that Nepali speakers call the language “Magar Kura” while Magar speakers call it “Magar Dhut” (1971). All the varieties of Magar are linguistically classified as: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Central Himalayan, Kham-Magar, Magar (Ethnologue 2013). Magar is non-tonal, though breathiness is phonemic, possibly indicating that Magar once was a tonal language (Shepherd 1971; Grunow-Hårsta 2008: 32). Magar is an agglutinative language (prefixes, suffixes, circumfixes) and contains a subject-object-verb grammatical structure (Grunow-Hårsta 2008: 32).
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; contrastive breathy vs clear phonation (register) treated as segmental/phonemic breathiness; possible former tone (second-hand, after Shepherd 1971 and Grunow-Hårsta 2008: 32).
